newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG's Chan stands firm, refusing to resign.
newsitem.headline: PNG's Chan stands firm, refusing to resign.

text.p: Besieged Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan on Sunday stood firm and refused to resign in the face of growing political calls for his removal ahead of Tuesday's rebel military deadline to quit.
"I am not going to step aside," Chan said in an address to the nation on television.
"We must uphold the constitution of Papua New Guinea. The constitution means democracy...I swore to it, I have to live by it," Chan said.
But on Sunday, calls mounted for Chan to resign over his plan to use foreign mercenaries to end the nine-year secessionist conflict on the copper-rich island of Bougainville.
Sir Michael Somare, the country's first prime minister after independence in 1975 and a person regarded as the father of the nation, said the mercenary plan was "stupid".
"The government made a stupid mistake...Sir Julius should resign," said Somare, calling for a caretaker government which would create an independent inquiry into the mercenary deal.
Chan has already announced an inquiry.
Political and military leaders agreed on Sunday that what started as an army revolt against Chan had now become a political crisis, which must be solved by politicians, not force.

"We have a major political crisis. There is absolutely no coup," said rebel army chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok, who ignited the crisis last Monday when he called on Chan to resign over the mercenary issue.
Singirok said the US$36 million contract with British-based military consultancy Sandline International, which provided 70 mercenaries, was unlawful and that those involved were corrupt.
Singirok was sacked, sparking an army revolt calling for his reinstatement and Chan's resignation by next Tuesday when parliament resumes for the last time ahead of June elections.
Street protests in support of the rebel officers erupted into two days of violence and looting in Port Moresby. But tight security has since seen the capital calm for four days.

All the mercenaries except their leader, former British colonel Tim Spicer, have been thrown out of the country by rebel army officers. Spicer is holed up in the residence of the British High Commissioner Bob Lowe, pending a court appearance on Monday over minor firearms charges.
Opposition political leaders on Sunday said they would move a motion in parliament on Tuesday requesting Chan to resign.
"Although we can't force him to resign constitutionally, we are trying to force him out morally," said John Momis, the MP for South Bougainville.
"Papua New Guinea is at the crossroads now and I think it is about time we forgot our political differences and put Papua New Guinea right," Momis told a news conference.

Chan's coalition government controls about 70 percent of the 109-seat unicameral parliament, but allegiances shift easily in this South Pacific nation which has a reputation for political instability.
Attending an emotional prayer service inside Murray Barracks, the nation's army headquarters, Singirok said he hoped there would be no more violence on Tuesday.
"I do not know what will happen, I cannot foretell," he said. "But we should not over-exaggerate the situation here in Papua New Guinea."
